planting.note: Plant container-grown or grafted trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, choosing a sheltered site away from frost pockets since open flowers are vulnerable to a late freeze.

directions: Magnolia sprengeri is a deciduous flowering tree native to open woodlands and valleys of central China, introduced to Western cultivation through seed collections made in the early twentieth century. Large, fragrant, cup-to-saucer-shaped flowers ranging from pale pink to deep rose appear on bare branches in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, with considerable color variation between individual seedlings, which is why later growers selected and named standout clones for consistent color and form. Over time it develops into a broad, round-headed tree of significant size, so give it a permanent, open site with room to mature and protection from the latest spring frosts that can brown open blooms. Once established it needs little beyond deep watering during dry spells and a mulched root zone to thrive for decades.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Queen's Lace Crape Myrtle (Red-and-White Picotee Tree-Form Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Give this full-size tree-form crape myrtle generous open space away from structures, since it eventually reaches 16 feet or more in height and spread.

directions: Queen's Lace grows into a substantial specimen tree, eventually reaching 16 feet or more, and produces the same striking red-centered, white-edged picotee flower clusters that made its dwarf sport Prairie Lace popular, but on a much larger, upright framework. New foliage opens coppery bronze before deepening to green for summer, then turns red, orange, and yellow in fall, while the maturing trunk develops exfoliating bark in gray, beige, and brown patches. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and allow room to either side for its eventual wide canopy; it makes a strong stand-alone specimen or a spaced allee along a driveway. Prune only to remove dead, crossing, or low sucker growth in late winter, since the unusual picotee bloom color is best displayed on an untopped, naturally vase-shaped canopy.

common_name: Tuscany Rose (Old Velvet Rose, Historic Dark Maroon Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Recorded in English gardens since at least the sixteenth century and long nicknamed the Old Velvet Rose, Tuscany is one of the oldest identifiable Gallica cultivars still in commerce, predating the larger-flowered nineteenth-century form later sold as Tuscany Superb. It bears semi-double blooms in the deepest velvety maroon-purple of any old garden rose, the near-black petals set off by a bold central cluster of golden stamens, and carries a rich, classic old-rose fragrance. Like other Gallicas it flowers only once, in a heavy, fragrant flush in late spring, on a compact, upright, suckering shrub that tolerates lean soil and considerable neglect. It needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay dense and productive.
sources: Graham Stuart Thomas, The Old Shrub Roses

common_name: Climbing Lady Hillingdon Rose (Vigorous Climbing Sport of Lady Hillingdon)

planting.note: Plant own-root stock against a sturdy trellis, wall, or pergola in spring or fall; give it several years to establish before expecting its full climbing size.

directions: Discovered in 1917 as a climbing sport of the bush Tea rose Lady Hillingdon, this vigorous climber carries the same elegant, loosely double, apricot-yellow blooms with a rich tea fragrance and distinctive plum-purple young stems, but on long canes capable of covering a substantial wall, pergola, or fence. It flowers heaviest in a strong spring flush with lighter repeat bloom through summer and fall, and like the bush form it shows good resistance to blackspot in humid climates compared with modern hybrid teas. Tie canes to their support as they grow, training them as horizontally as practical to encourage more flowering side shoots along the length of the plant. Prune only lightly to remove dead or crossing wood, since hard pruning sacrifices much of the framework the climbing habit depends on.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Set out container-grown or rooted-cutting plants in spring once frost danger has passed, since late freezes can damage the early flush of new growth.

directions: Native to the Amur River region and Korea, this wild species deutzia is one of the hardier members of the genus and served as the pollen parent behind Victor Lemoine's pink-flowered hybrid Deutzia x kalmiiflora. It forms an upright, multi-stemmed shrub with peeling second-year bark, covered in early summer by rounded two- to three-inch clusters of small, half-inch white flowers. Site it in full sun to light shade in ordinary, well-drained garden soil, and expect best performance in climates with a distinct cold winter rather than mild coastal regions, where late-spring frosts can nip emerging shoots. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes at the base right after flowering, since like other deutzia it sets next year's buds on the current season's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, giving the arching branches room to spread.

directions: Collected in Yunnan by the French missionary-botanist Abbe Delavay in the 1880s, this wild species deutzia carries three-quarter-inch flowers that open white on the inner face and flush purple on the reverse, held in rounded clusters in early June. It served as seed parent for several of Lemoine's celebrated hybrids, including the pink-flowered Deutzia x kalmiiflora and the elegantissima group, thanks to its distinctively colored, purple-backed petals. The shrub grows into a substantial six- to seven-foot mound with pale, slightly scurfy young shoots, so give it a background position in a mixed border or shrub screen rather than a tight foundation spot. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and renew the plant after flowering by removing a portion of the oldest stems at ground level.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil, choosing a site with room for its arching, medium-sized habit.

directions: Introduced from western China by plant hunter Ernest Wilson in 1905, this wild species deutzia is one of the direct parents behind the large Deutzia x hybrida group of Lemoine hybrids, including Perle Rose. Inch-wide, pale purplish-rose flowers that fade toward the petal margins open in two- to three-inch clusters at the ends of short twigs in June, later than many spring-blooming shrubs. Its narrow, lance-shaped leaves and arching branch habit give it a softer, more graceful outline than the coarser-textured Deutzia scabra. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin out some of the oldest wood at the base right after flowering to keep the shrub renewing well.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil, siting in full sun for the strongest bloom.

directions: First described by botanist William Hemsley in 1887 from specimens collected in central and western China, this wild species deutzia bears three-inch corymbs of half- to one-inch flowers that range from white to soft pink, opening on shrubs with pale, peeling grey-brown bark. For decades it was credited as a parent of several Lemoine hybrid deutzias, but later botanical review showed that those crosses actually trace back to the related species Deutzia purpurascens, which Lemoine and Franchet had mistakenly treated as a variety of discolor. Narrow, dull-green leaves covered in fine starlike hairs give the foliage a soft, felted texture through the growing season. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and renew the shrub after flowering by cutting out a share of the oldest canes at the base.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
